chapters.title: Chapter 5: Carry and Cross-Asset Value Strategies

lessons.title: Carry in Commodities: Contango, Backwardation, and the Roll Yield

body.text: Currency carry gave this course one bet. Commodities give it several, gold, silver, and crude do not always sit in the same curve state at the same time, which means a commodity carry strategy has something a single-pair USD-INR strategy structurally cannot: genuine cross-sectional breadth.

children.text: Chapter 2's commodities lesson defined contango and backwardation and explained why the futures curve, not just spot price, drives a large part of a commodity position's true return. This lesson turns that concept into a signal: quantifying roll yield precisely, sizing positions from it, and applying it across gold, silver, and crude simultaneously, directly addressing the single-bet limitation Lesson 2 flagged for currency carry.
From Curve Shape to Signal: Quantifying Roll Yield

Roll yield measures the actual return earned or lost purely from rolling a futures position from the expiring near-month contract into the next one, holding spot price fixed. It can be read directly off the two nearest listed contract prices, without needing a full model of storage costs or convenience yield, since the curve itself already encodes those.

body.caption: Annualized roll yield from the two nearest futures contracts. Positive when the near-month contract trades above the far-month (backwardation, a long position is paid to roll), negative when it trades below (contango, a long position pays to roll).

children.text: The Signal: Position Sized by Roll Yield Magnitude, Not Just Its Sign

A binary long-if-backwardation, short-if-contango rule throws away useful information. A mildly negative roll yield and a steeply negative one both say "short," but they are not equally attractive opportunities. Sizing the position by roll yield magnitude, scaled by the asset's volatility using the same vol-targeting framework from Chapter 4 and Lesson 2's currency carry-to-vol approach, produces a more graduated signal: strong backwardation earns a larger long position, mild contango a smaller short one, rather than treating every non-zero roll yield reading identically.
Applying It Across Gold, Silver, and Crude Simultaneously

body.caption: Illustrative Roll Yield Snapshot Across Three MCX Commodities

body.text: These prices and resulting roll yields are illustrative, chosen to demonstrate the calculation and show a realistic mix of curve states, not actual quoted MCX contract prices on any specific date.

This is the breadth advantage Lesson 2 said currency carry structurally lacks. Here, three genuinely different commodities show three different signals, two short, one long, at the same moment, exactly the kind of independent, non-uniform bet set the Fundamental Law of Active Management rewards. A single USD-INR position can never offer this on its own.

children.text: When Roll Yield and Trend Disagree

Nothing guarantees a commodity's roll yield signal and its trend signal from Chapter 4 point the same direction. Crude can sit in contango, a bearish carry signal, while its price is in a strong, sustained uptrend, a bullish trend signal, at the exact same time; oversupply pushing far-month prices up relative to near-month says one thing about the curve while strong recent demand says another about price direction. This is not a bug to be resolved by force, it is two independent views on the same instrument, and Lesson 5 covers the principled way to combine them.

body.text: Do not resolve a carry-trend disagreement by simply netting the two signals against each other with no explicit rule, or worse, by running both signals at full, unadjusted size on the same instrument simultaneously. Either approach can produce a position size and direction nobody actually intended. Lesson 5 builds a proper combination framework; until then, treat carry and trend as separate, independently risk-budgeted views.

children.text: Practical Mechanics: Realized Roll Yield vs a Curve Snapshot

A signal calculated from today's curve snapshot is not the same as the return actually realized when a position is rolled, since the curve can shift between when the signal is measured and when the roll is executed, and the roll itself, like any trade, incurs slippage. This echoes Chapter 1's landscape lesson: a backtest that assumes costless, instant execution at the exact snapshot price will systematically overstate real roll yield capture, particularly in a fast-moving commodity like crude where the curve can reshape meaningfully within days.

body.title: The Crude Position With Two Signals and No Rule
body.scenario: A junior quant researcher's crude oil model generates a full-size long position from a strong trend signal, and separately, a full-size short position from a steep contango carry signal, on the same day. With no combination rule in place, they simply net the two signals by subtracting one from the other, producing a small residual long position, and treat this as the final answer.
body.prompt: What is the problem with resolving the disagreement this way, based on this lesson's warning?
body.modelAnswer: Naively netting two full-size, independently generated signals against each other does not represent a deliberate risk decision, it is an accidental byproduct of how the two signals happened to be scaled relative to each other, which could easily have produced a large net position instead of a small one if the underlying numbers had been slightly different. Trend and carry are answering genuinely different questions, whether price is likely to keep moving in its recent direction versus whether the position is being compensated for holding it through the roll, and treating them as directly subtractable implies they are measuring the same thing on the same scale, which this lesson explicitly says they are not. The correct approach, covered fully in Lesson 5, is to treat carry and trend as separate, independently risk-budgeted views and combine them through an explicit, deliberate weighting scheme, not an arbitrary netting of whatever sizes each signal happened to generate.

body.title: Computing Roll Yield
body.prompt: Crude's near-month futures contract trades at ₹6,200 per barrel, while the contract one month out trades at ₹6,100. Using roll yield ≈ (F_near - F_far)/F_far × (365/days), with days = 30, what is the annualized roll yield (%)? Round to one decimal place.
body.explanation: (6200 - 6100) / 6100 × (365/30) = (100/6100) × 12.1667 ≈ 0.0164 × 12.1667 ≈ 0.1995, or about 19.9%. The positive sign confirms backwardation, the near-month contract trading above the far-month, meaning a long position is compensated for rolling forward.

body.title: Why Commodities Offer More Breadth Than Currency Carry
body.question: Based on this lesson, why does a commodity carry strategy trading gold, silver, and crude simultaneously offer more genuine breadth than a USD-INR-only currency carry strategy?
options: Because commodities are always more volatile than currencies
Because the three commodities can show genuinely different, independent curve states and carry signals at the same time, unlike a single currency pair which is structurally one bet
Because MCX has better execution technology than NSE
Because commodity carry does not involve any risk premium
body.explanation: This lesson's illustrative table showed gold and silver in contango while crude sat in backwardation at the same moment, three genuinely different, independently-driven carry signals. A single USD-INR position cannot replicate this, since it is fundamentally one instrument with one carry reading at a time, exactly the breadth limitation Lesson 2 identified.

points: Roll yield can be read directly from the two nearest futures contracts, positive in backwardation, negative in contango, without needing a full storage-cost model
Sizing by roll yield magnitude, not just its sign, produces a more graduated signal than a binary long-or-short rule
Gold, silver, and crude can show genuinely different curve states simultaneously, giving commodity carry real cross-sectional breadth that single-pair currency carry structurally lacks
Carry and trend signals on the same commodity can disagree, since they measure genuinely different things, and should not be naively netted against each other without an explicit combination rule
A curve snapshot is not the same as realized roll yield; execution timing and slippage on the actual roll matter, echoing Chapter 1's emphasis on realistic execution assumptions
Lesson 5 builds the principled framework for combining carry and trend signals that this lesson's disagreement scenario sets up
